subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on theories of media effects, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain theories of media effects for GCSE Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Types of media: traditional versus new (digital) media
Ownership and control: pluralist versus Marxist/manipulative views
Media representations of gender, age, ethnicity and class
Theories of media effects: the hypodermic syringe model
Theories of media effects: the uses and gratifications model
Theories of media effects: audience decoding and the reception model

questions.lo: Types of media: traditional versus new (digital) media
questions.q: Which of the following is an example of 'new' (digital) media rather than 'traditional' media?
options: A terrestrial radio broadcast
A printed newspaper
A social media platform
A cinema film reel
questions.explain: New media are digital, interactive and often user-generated, such as social media, streaming and websites. Printed newspapers, cinema and traditional broadcast radio are examples of traditional media.

questions.lo: Types of media: traditional versus new (digital) media
questions.q: A key feature that makes new media different from traditional media is that new media are:
options: Only available in print
Controlled entirely by the government
Interactive, allowing audiences to create and respond to content
Unable to reach large audiences
questions.explain: New media are interactive and often two-way: audiences can produce, share and comment on content. Traditional media tend to be one-way, transmitting content from producer to a passive audience.

questions.lo: Ownership and control: pluralist versus Marxist/manipulative views
questions.q: The pluralist view of media ownership and control argues that:
options: The media give audiences a wide range of choices and reflect what audiences want
The media have no influence on society at all
Only the state should own all media
A small ruling class uses the media to brainwash the public
questions.explain: Pluralists argue that media content responds to audience demand and offers diverse viewpoints, so power is spread out. Audiences choose freely and owners must give the public what it wants.

questions.lo: Ownership and control: pluralist versus Marxist/manipulative views
questions.q: The Marxist (manipulative) view of media ownership argues that:
options: Owners use the media to spread ruling-class ideology and maintain their power
Media ownership is spread evenly across society
The media never contain any bias
The media simply mirror what audiences want
questions.explain: Marxists argue that a small number of wealthy owners control the media and use it to transmit ruling-class ideology, shaping public opinion in ways that protect their interests and the capitalist system.

questions.lo: Ownership and control: pluralist versus Marxist/manipulative views
questions.q: A sociologist argues that because a few powerful companies own most newspapers and TV channels, the public only hears a narrow range of views. This argument is closest to the:
options: Marxist / manipulative view
Pluralist view
Uses and gratifications model
Functionalist view of value consensus
questions.explain: Concern that concentrated ownership limits diversity and lets owners shape opinion is a Marxist/manipulative argument, in contrast to pluralists who stress choice and audience power.

questions.lo: Media representations of gender, age, ethnicity and class
questions.q: A 'stereotype' in media representation is:
options: An oversimplified, fixed image of a social group repeated in the media
An accurate, detailed portrayal of a whole social group
A type of camera used in filming
A method of measuring audience size
questions.explain: A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified image of a social group. The media are often criticised for repeating stereotypes of women, ethnic minorities, the young and old, and social classes.

questions.lo: Media representations of gender, age, ethnicity and class
questions.q: Feminists such as those who study the media argue that women are often shown in a limited range of roles. Which is the best example of this criticism?
options: Women shown mainly as mothers, homemakers or in terms of their appearance
Women shown as leaders in every news story
Women completely absent from all media
Women only shown as scientists and politicians
questions.explain: Feminist analysis highlights how women are frequently represented in narrow, traditional roles (domestic, decorative or defined by looks), which can reinforce patriarchal ideas about gender.

questions.lo: Media representations of gender, age, ethnicity and class
questions.q: News coverage that repeatedly links a particular ethnic group with crime is an example of:
options: Uses and gratifications
A negative or stereotyped media representation
Positive representation
The pluralist model
questions.explain: Consistently associating an ethnic group with crime is a negative, stereotyped representation. Sociologists argue such representations can shape public attitudes and reinforce prejudice.

questions.lo: Theories of media effects: the hypodermic syringe model
questions.q: The hypodermic syringe (or 'magic bullet') model of media effects claims that:
options: The media have no effect on behaviour
The media 'inject' messages directly into a passive audience who are strongly affected
Audiences use the media only for relaxation
Audiences actively interpret media in different ways
questions.explain: The hypodermic syringe model sees the audience as passive and easily influenced: media messages are 'injected' directly and have a powerful, immediate effect on attitudes and behaviour.

questions.lo: Theories of media effects: the hypodermic syringe model
questions.q: Which criticism is most commonly made of the hypodermic syringe model?
options: It wrongly assumes audiences are passive and all react in the same way
It only applies to newspapers
It gives the audience too much power
It denies that the media exist
questions.explain: Critics argue the hypodermic model treats audiences as passive and identical, ignoring that people interpret media differently and are influenced by other factors such as family and peers.

questions.lo: Theories of media effects: the uses and gratifications model
questions.q: The uses and gratifications model argues that audiences:
options: Are passively injected with media messages
Are completely controlled by media owners
Never use the media at all
Actively choose and use media to satisfy their own needs, such as entertainment or information
questions.explain: The uses and gratifications model sees audiences as active. People select media to meet needs such as information, entertainment, personal identity and social interaction, rather than being passive victims.

questions.lo: Theories of media effects: the uses and gratifications model
questions.q: A person watches the news to keep informed and streams comedy to relax. According to the uses and gratifications model, they are:
options: Proving that the media have no effect
Being manipulated by a hypodermic syringe effect
Rejecting all media messages
Actively using different media to satisfy different needs
questions.explain: This is a clear example of uses and gratifications: the audience member actively selects media for particular purposes (information and relaxation), showing an active rather than passive audience.

questions.lo: Theories of media effects: audience decoding and the reception model
questions.q: The reception (decoding) model of media effects argues that audiences:
options: Are simply injected with messages
Cannot understand any media messages
All understand a media message in exactly the same way
Interpret or 'decode' media messages in different ways depending on their background
questions.explain: The reception/decoding model (associated with Stuart Hall) argues audiences actively decode messages. They may accept, negotiate or reject the intended meaning depending on their social position and experiences.

questions.lo: Theories of media effects: audience decoding and the reception model
questions.q: Two viewers watch the same advert: one accepts its message, the other rejects it as misleading. This difference best supports the:
options: Reception / decoding model
Hypodermic syringe model
Idea that the media have no effect
Marxist manipulative model
questions.explain: Different interpretations of the same content support the reception model: audiences decode messages differently (accepting, negotiating or rejecting them) rather than all being affected identically.

questions.lo: Moral panics and folk devils
questions.q: A 'moral panic' is best defined as:
options: A type of media ownership
A brief news story that is quickly forgotten
An exaggerated public reaction, amplified by the media, to a group or activity seen as a threat to society
A method of measuring crime accurately
questions.explain: A moral panic is an exaggerated, media-driven reaction to a perceived threat to social values. The concept is associated with Stanley Cohen's study of Mods and Rockers.

questions.lo: Moral panics and folk devils
questions.q: Within a moral panic, a 'folk devil' is:
options: The group identified and demonised as the source of the threat
A journalist who reports the story
The audience watching the news
A government official
questions.explain: A folk devil is the group blamed and demonised during a moral panic (for example, a particular youth subculture), portrayed by the media as a danger to society's values.

questions.lo: Moral panics and folk devils
questions.q: Repeated, exaggerated media coverage of a youth group leads to public alarm, more police attention and even more reporting. This spiral is known as:
options: Deviancy amplification
Value consensus
Uses and gratifications
The digital divide
questions.explain: Deviancy amplification is when media reaction increases the very behaviour it condemns, feeding a moral panic. Cohen showed how coverage of Mods and Rockers amplified the perceived problem.

questions.lo: The media and globalisation
questions.q: How has globalisation affected the media?
options: It has made all media purely local
It has removed all media ownership
It has ended the use of digital media
It has allowed media content and culture to spread rapidly across the world
questions.explain: Globalisation, driven by new digital technology, allows media content, brands and culture to cross borders quickly, linking audiences worldwide and spreading shared cultural products.

questions.lo: The media and globalisation
questions.q: The concern that global media spread the culture of powerful Western nations and threaten local cultures is known as:
options: Value consensus
The digital divide
The uses and gratifications model
Cultural imperialism
questions.explain: Cultural imperialism is the idea that global media export dominant (often Western) culture, potentially eroding or homogenising local cultures and identities.

questions.lo: The media and globalisation
questions.q: The gap between those who have good access to new digital media and those who do not is called the:
options: Moral panic
Folk devil
Digital divide
Correspondence principle
questions.explain: The digital divide refers to inequality in access to digital technology and the internet, often linked to income, age or global region, so not everyone benefits equally from new media.
